body.p: The non-final Office Action dated June 20, 2024, has been received and carefully noted. The above amendments to the claims, and the following remarks, are submitted as a full and complete response thereto.

Claims 1, 2, and 23 have been amended for further clarity. No claims have been cancelled. No claims have been added. No new matter is added. Claims 1-26 are currently pending in the application, of which claims 1, 12, and 20 are independent claims. Further examination and reconsideration of the application is respectfully requested.

Applicant notes with Appreciation the Office Action's indication on page 5 that claims 15- 18, 21, 22, and 24 recite allowable subject matter. Applicant also respectfully notes that claims 5- 8 and 23 were not rejected on art-based grounds, so Applicant respectfully submits that these claims are also allowable when the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) is overcome. Applicant kindly thanks the Examiner for the assistance. Applicant respectfully submits that all of the claims
are allowable at least in view of the following.

On page 2, the Office Action rejected claims 1-11 and 23 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter of the invention.
With respect to claims 1 and 2, Applicant has added reference numerals to further clarify what "both" pertains to in these claims.
With respect to claim 23, Applicant has removed "the" before "validation".
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejection has been overcome and respectfully requests that the rejection be withdrawn.

On pages 3-5, the Office Action rejected claims 1-4, 9-14, 19, 20, 25, and 26 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by Weinert, Jr. et al. (U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2020/0004798). Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection.
As disclosed in paragraph [0002] of the subject application:

Currently, different versions of RPA workflows are developed for different targets, such as Windows®, Mac®, Linux®, a mobile operating system (OS), etc. Thus, multiple versions [of workflows] are generated for the same automation. This is cumbersome and leads to project and library multiplicity, as well as more difficulty with version control, bug fixes, and updates. Furthermore, RPA

p.u: activities do not currently have functionality to specify target platforms.

body.p: Emphasis added.

Some embodiments allow multiple target platforms to be handled in the same pro ject. The target platform(s) can be specified at the automation and/or activity level in order to provide the supported functionality for each. This may also allow previously built automations to be applied to new target frameworks without
starting from scratch.

Paragraph [0027] of the subject application, emphasis added. "[E]ach activity may have a tag, a variable, an array, or some other descriptor or data structure that specifies the target platform(s) for a given activity." Paragraph [0028] of the subject application. "Native functionality may be used for the given target. This native functionality may be used to provide OS-dependent
functionality, including full desktop interaction between the user and the automation, for
example." Paragraph [0033] of the subject application.
Along these lines, independent claim 1 recites, in part, "(a) configur[ing] an RPA project
in accordance with a target platform configuration comprising a plurality of target platforms, (b)
configur[ing] multiple versions of one or more activities for the respective target platform for the
respective version, or (c) both (a) and (b)." Independent claims 12 and 20, which each have their
own scope, recite similar features to (a) and (b), respectively. In rejecting these features, the Office
Action, on page 2, relied on paragraphs [0011]-[0016] of Weinert, Jr. et al. for (a) and on paragraph
[0017] of (b). Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. fails to disclose all of the
features in the rejected claims, both explicitly, and implicitly.
Weinert, Jr. et al. generally discusses that:

Embodiments as disclosed provide improved RPA systems and methods that utilize a set of reusable modules. These modules may include an associated set of configurable parameters and be associated with instructions for a browser automation platform. An RPA application to accomplish a task at a target website is built using these modules. The RPA application may be executed at the RPA system using an instance of a browser. The RPA application can be executed by evaluating an identified module of the RPA application based on the configuration parameters to determine instructions for a browser automation platform for the identified module. These browser automation platform instructions can then be provided to the browser automation platform to execute
against the browser instance.
Abstract, emphasis added.

Embodiments of the systems and methods presented herein may make use of an abstraction layer comprising of "handlers" that provide a high-level wrapper around specific points of robotic process automation. Instead of using raw coded scripts to interact with a specific robotic process automation platform, a user interface allows a user to build robotically automated processes that conform to the handlers of an abstraction layer. The automation application thus remains
vendor and platform agnostic.

Accordingly, embodiment may offer a number of advantages, including improving the maintainability and scalability of a system dealing with thousands of automated processes and increasing the feasibility (e.g., financially or otherwise) of supporting such systems due at least to the drastic decrease in the amount of time and experience required to build, maintain, and deploy these robotically automated processes. Additionally, the flexibility of being able to migrate to an entirely new underlying technology drastically increases the longevity of systems coded
according to embodiment of such a proprietary abstraction layer.

Applicant respectfully submits that a web browser is not a target platform. Rather, the web
browser is an application. As disclosed in paragraph [0026] of the subject application, example
target platforms include "legacy targets, .NET Core, cross-platform (e.g., able to run on both
Windows® and Linux®), Apple® OS X, native mobile, and the like." In other words, applications
run on platforms. A problem with conventional approaches, including that discussed in Weinert,
Jr. et al., is that "multiple versions of the same automation are created for each platform." See Id.
Per the above, paragraphs [0014] and [0016] of Weinert, Jr. et al. discuss "creating a first job
execution instance for the first RPA application" and "creating a second job execution instance for

the second RPA application", respectively. Thus, there are multiple RPA applications for multiple web browsers, and a single projection does not handle multiple platforms. This is unlike the claimed features discussed above, where a developer can create a workflow in a project that would work for multiple target platforms, such as running on both Windows® and Linux®.

With respect to "configur[ing] multiple versions of one or more activities for the respective target platform for the respective version," as claimed, Applicant respectfully submits that it is helpful to first look at what activities and RPA workflows are. As disclosed and defined in the subject application, "[t]he automation project enables automation of rule-based processes by giving the developer control of the execution order and the relationship between a custom set of steps developed in a workflow, defined herein as 'activities.' One commercial example of an embodiment of designer 110 is UiPath StudioTM." See paragraph [0035]. "[RPA r]obots 130 are execution agents that run workflows built in designer 110." See paragraph [0041] of the subject application.

Applicant respectfully notes that Weinert, Jr. et al. does not mention RPA workflows or the activities (steps) included therein. It is unclear from the disclosure of Weinert, Jr. et al. whether and how a user could create such workflows using the system thereof. Also, per Weinert, Jr. et al, the goal is to create an abstraction layer to "provide a high level wrapper around specific points of robotic process automation." See paragraph [0011]. A user selects the desired module for the and defines a value for a desired website. See paragraphs [0013] and [0015] of Weinert, Jr. et al. A user would not be able to create a single button click activity, for example, that would work on any respective target platform that is supported.

The Office Action, on page 2, alleged that "activities are interpreted to correspond to determining values specific to user and context; versions are interpreted to correspond to the activities for first value and second value respectively". However, per the above, activities are steps in RPA workflows, such as clicking a button, opening a file, etc. Also, assuming arguendo that determining values specific to a user and context could be interpreted as an activity when accorded its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as it would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, there is no disclosure in Weinert, Jr. et al. of these being part of a workflow. Furthermore, Applicant respectfully submits that versions would be interpreted differently. "Version" is a term of art pertaining to a given release of a software application as it is modified over time (e.g., v1, v2.3.1, etc.). Applicant respectfully submits that the first and second values of Weinert, Jr. et al. do not pertain to activities (i.e., steps in RPA workflows).
Thus, Applicant respectfully submits that the independent claims patentably distinguish over Weinert, Jr. et al.

Claims 2-4, 9-11, 13, 14, 19, 25, and 26 depend from independent claim 1, 12, or 26 and inherit the patentable features thereof. At least by virtue of their dependencies, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 2-4, 9-11, 13, 14, 19, 25, and 26 also patentably distinguish over Weinert, Jr. et al.

Furthermore, with respect to claim 3, the claim recites, in part, that "the target platform configuration is or comprises a global scope for the RPA project that generates activities for the plurality of different target platforms automatically within a scope of the RPA workflow." Claim 13, which has its own scope, recites similar features. In rejecting these features, the Office Action,
on page 4, relied on paragraph [0011] of Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. fails to disclose these features, both explicitly and implicitly.

Applicant respectfully submits that there is no automatic generation of activities, nor is there a mention of RPA workflows in Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant also respectfully submits that in addition to these features not being mentioned in Weinert, Jr. et al., there is no global scope that automatically generates such activities for a plurality of different target platforms, as claimed. In Weinert, Jr. et al., one cannot develop a single RPA workflow and have it work for multiple operating systems, for instance.
Applicant respectfully submits that similar issues also exist with respect to the other rejected dependent claims

Applicant further respectfully notes that a claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference. See Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil Co. of California, 814 F.2d 628, 631, 2 USPQ2d 1051, 1053 (Fed. Cir. 1987), emphasis added. When a claim covers several structures or compositions, either generically or as alternatives, the claim is deemed anticipated if any of the structures or compositions within the scope of the claim is known in the prior art. See Brown v. 3M, 265 F.3d 1349, 1351, 60 USPQ2d 1375, 1376 (Fed. Cir. 2001). The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim. See Richardson v. Suzuki Motor Co., 868 F.2d 1226, 1236, 9 USPQ2d 1913, 1920 (Fed. Cir. 1989), emphasis added. The claimed features discussed above are missing from Weinert, Jr. et al., and furthermore, the features are not presented in as complete detail as claimed. As such, Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. explicitly cannot anticipate all of the features recited in the rejected claims.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejection has been overcome and respectfully requests that the rejection be withdrawn.

In view of the above, Applicant respectfully submits that the present application is in condition for allowance. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the claims be allowed and the application be passed to issue.

Although Applicant has focused the remarks and/or amendments on or primarily on the independent claims in order to expedite the prosecution of the instant application, Applicant reserves the right to remark on and/or amend any of the dependent claims at any time. The mere fact that Applicant has not remarked on and/or amended any of the dependent claims at this time, either related to an Official Notice or not, is unequivocally not an admission of prior art.

Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are not patentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application.

Applicant reserves the right to pursue at a later date any previously pending or other broader or narrower claims that capture any subject matter supported by the present disclosure, including subject matter found to be specifically disclaimed herein or by any prior prosecution.

Accordingly, reviewers of this or any parent, child or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.
